claims.text: Overall degradation during tribo-corrosion of high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between passive-oxide formation and mechanical oxide removal.
Faster formation of a self-repairing oxide film mitigates tribo-corrosion degradation.
Excessive mechanical removal of the passive oxide accelerates degradation.
The initial high-entropy alloy surface has a naturally formed, uniform passive oxide layer.
Temperature or alloying-element changes can vary the rate of oxide regeneration.
Passive-film morphology, density, and thickness mediate the tribo-corrosion response.
Mechanical wear removes the protective oxide film during tribo-corrosion.
Intrinsic oxidation of the alloy reforms the mechanically removed film.
Net degradation is determined by whether the oxide film can re-establish before it is removed again.
When oxide formation outpaces mechanical removal, the passive film limits both metal loss by wear and electrochemical attack.
When mechanical removal outpaces oxide regeneration, loss of the protective barrier enhances degradation.
A rapidly reforming oxide film can make total tribo-corrosion degradation lower than degradation measured under isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Aggressive mechanical oxide removal will significantly elevate both wear and corrosion.
The proposed behavior should hold where oxidation kinetics are the primary surface-recovery mechanism.
The proposed behavior may fail under high stress, in highly aggressive media, or in alloys that do not form robust oxides.
Localized pitting or phase instability can displace passive-film regeneration as the dominant control of tribo-corrosion.
Prior studies on similar systems support the qualitative interplay between oxide regeneration and mechanical removal.
A lack of significant correlation between oxide-regeneration behavior and combined degradation would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
